doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Train to Great Lakes; Clark Terry's bunk; Camp Robert Smalls
summary: The band rides to Great Lakes in a private car, sleeps in Clark Terry's bunk, and hears of the ship's company band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: three years at St. Mary’s College. See we went in, when they called us we were all put on temporary leave when they first recruited us. Then when they told us okay it’s time, then we got on the train and this was in 1945 [sic] around October, maybe the first of October, yeah, got on the train, the Western Pacific, and took off for Chicago. Well there was a jam session going on where the guys had their books out and they were having jam sessions on the train. Because we had a private car. And they had one compartment in it, that’s where the Chief stayed. And so the guys made so much noise. One day the Chief said, “Okay, no more sessions.” Because it was a three day trip. So I think after about the middle of the second day, so we traveled and we went to oh Omaha and Salt Lake City, Denver, and finally we landed in Chicago. So we got off the train in Chicago. And there we are standing on the platform, so we had to go out to what they called the North Side, because that’s where the Great Lakes training station was. So we were all standing on the platform. So then this truck came and took us out to the Great Lakes. Now they had two separate camps. Camp Robert Smalls, that’s the black camp. And then the Great Lakes Naval Training Station, that was the white side. So we had to wait, I don’t know, but we had to wait for something. So we’re standing up there in our California clothes and that wind, you know that Chicago wind, whoooo — it would go right up your pants leg you know. So anyhow, but finally they got us inside and they found a barracks for us. Assigned us bunks and everything. And they didn’t have enough bunks. See they have some bunks and hammocks. So what they did with me, see I’m W, I’m way down on the list because they process you alphabetically. So see they didn’t have any bunks. So what they did they said well one of our — we’ve got some of the fellas who were on leave and you can sleep in this fella’s bunk until he comes back. It turned out to be Clark Terry’s bunk. And this is 1942, and he hadn’t made a name for himself and we didn’t know one another. But when he came back naturally I had to give up the bunk. So I mentioned that to him when he was here at one of our clubs a few years back. And I had a picture of that band, I don’t know what I did with it, but I had a picture of the band, the Great Lakes Band, I had a picture of that. I don’t know where I got it from but it was a copy. I don’t know where I got it from. I think I gave it to him.
Boy that name has come up a lot, that place near Chicago where all the servicemen—

Camp Robert Smalls. And their ship’s company band was a dynamite band. Clark Terry was in it, Osie Johnson the drummer was in it, Willie Smith was in it for a short time. They say he got out on a Section 8 so I guess he put on a pretty good act. Yeah. And from there he went to Charlie Spivak’s band because the white bands were starting to integrate. So anyhow, at Great Lakes that’s when we got all the uniforms and everything and then the Chief, we had to learn how to march in formation, make your right turn, your left © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
